title: A voice becomes words.
intro: Imagine a small team inside your computer. One member listens, one understands, and one puts the words where you are typing.
story: Press the shortcut and VOCO starts listening. It turns your speech into words on your own computer and pastes them at your cursor while you are still talking. Press the shortcut again and VOCO finishes the last words.
Each part of VOCO does one job and passes small messages to the next. Sound travels in packets of one tenth of a second, so words can appear before you finish a sentence.

Nothing you say leaves the computer. The speech model runs on the processor, and the only network request VOCO makes by itself asks GitHub whether a new release exists. Later chapters open each box and show the real code inside.

steps.label: Shortcut
steps.detail: You press Super+X, or the shortcut you chose. The same shortcut, or Stop dictation in VOCO's menu, ends the recording.

steps.label: Microphone
steps.detail: VOCO records the microphone. On Wayland, Rust records through libpulse. On X11, the window records through a WebKit AudioWorklet.

steps.label: Speech model
steps.detail: A Python worker runs NVIDIA Nemotron Speech Streaming on the processor and answers with the transcript so far.

steps.label: Delivery
steps.detail: Only the new words move on. VOCO puts them on the clipboard, then presses Shift+Insert.

steps.label: Your cursor
steps.detail: The words land in whichever app has keyboard focus. VOCO never presses Enter for you.

facts.title: One warm worker
facts.text: The speech worker starts and loads its model when VOCO launches, then stays running between recordings. If it has exited, the next recording starts a fresh one.

facts.title: Words follow the focus
facts.text: VOCO doesn't remember where a recording started. Each group of words goes to whatever has keyboard focus when that group is ready.

facts.title: Local by design
facts.text: The window's content security policy allows connections only to VOCO itself, Tauri's message channel and api.github.com. Speech never needs the network.

facts.title: Stop finishes the job
facts.text: Stop sends the last audio, waits for the final transcript and pastes it. After a finished sentence it adds one space, so the next dictation starts apart. Words that couldn't be pasted are copied to the clipboard, and VOCO tells you.

title: Meet the languages.
intro: VOCO is one app written in several languages. Each language sits where it fits best.
story: Rust is the part the operating system sees. It starts processes, owns files and sockets, talks to the desktop and presses the paste keys.
The window is a small React app written in TypeScript. It runs inside WebKitGTK and can reach the system only through commands that Rust registers.

Speech recognition runs in a Python worker. A small C++ bridge connects it to NeMo-Speech.cpp, the native recognizer. Two optional extensions, one for GNOME Shell and one for Chromium, are written in JavaScript.

steps.detail: The Tauri 2 shell: processes, sockets, files, D-Bus, the tray, Wayland capture and paste.

steps.label: Python
steps.detail: The speech worker reads one JSON line and writes one JSON line for each request.

title: One press, one recording.
intro: A shortcut makes a small promise: one press starts a recording, and the next press finishes it.
story: A new setup uses Super+X. Change shortcut in VOCO's menu offers Super+X, Alt+D, Alt+Shift+D and Custom shortcut…, which opens the shortcut settings. A custom shortcut needs Alt, Control or Super plus one main key, and a shortcut you saved is never changed for you.

How the key press reaches VOCO depends on the desktop. On X11, VOCO grabs the shortcut. On Wayland, VOCO reads the keyboards for the three preset shortcuts, or the GNOME companion grabs them inside the Shell. The snap reads no keyboards, so on GNOME Wayland the companion or GNOME itself holds its shortcut.
Every route ends at the same gate. It ignores a second toggle that arrives within 120 ms of the first, so one press never counts twice.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: VOCO checks the saved shortcut at startup. An invalid one is reset to Super+X, and VOCO tells you why.

steps.label: Route
steps.detail: The press arrives through the X11 grab, the companion's grab, keyboard reading, the VOCO Dictation IBus input source, GNOME's own keyboard shortcut in the snap or voco --toggle.

steps.label: Consume
steps.detail: A grab keeps the keys away from other apps. Reading the keyboards only observes, so the focused app sees the keys too.

steps.label: Debounce
steps.detail: A toggle within 120 ms of the previous one is ignored.

steps.label: Toggle
steps.detail: The window starts or stops the recording. A toggle that arrives before the window is ready is kept and applied once it is.

facts.title: X11 toggles on release
facts.text: While the chord is held, VOCO's grab receives every key. VOCO waits for the release before it toggles, so the paste keys reach the app.

facts.title: Why Super+X
facts.text: The companion's grab and GNOME's keyboard shortcuts take only the chord's letter, so the focused app sees the modifier pressed and released alone. After a lone Alt, Firefox, Thunderbird, LibreOffice and Electron editors open their menu bar, which swallows the Shift+Insert pastes that follow. Those apps open no menu bar for a lone Super, and Mutter doesn't open the overview once it has seen the X.

facts.title: Passive keys also reach the app
facts.text: When VOCO reads the keyboards, the focused app gets the shortcut as well. With Alt+D, browsers move the cursor to the address bar, so your words land there, and terminals delete a word. Apps rarely act on Super+X, so for it VOCO says only that an app that has its own use for it acts on it too. Once per launch VOCO shows "Your shortcut also reached the app" with a way to avoid it.

facts.title: One toggle, however it arrives
facts.text: The GNOME companion holds a 2.5-second lease on the shortcut, and while it is fresh VOCO ignores the same keys from the keyboards. The IBus source holds a 1-second lease, and VOCO also releases its X11 grab so the source receives the keys.

facts.title: voco --toggle
facts.text: A desktop binding can run voco --toggle. It connects once to VOCO's owner-only socket, and the connection itself is the request. It never launches VOCO, changes focus or confirms whether recording started.

facts.title: Other shortcuts on Wayland
facts.text: Keyboard reading covers only Super+X, Alt+D and Alt+Shift+D, so any other shortcut on Wayland needs a desktop binding that runs voco --toggle. VOCO registers a shortcut through Tauri's global-shortcut plugin only outside Wayland, and only while no IBus source takes the chord. Whenever settings can't confirm that the shortcut works, they advise: "To dictate into other apps, start dictation from the tray or assign voco --toggle to a shortcut in your desktop settings."

facts.title: Reading keyboards
facts.text: VOCO reads the keyboards in /dev/input that can type one of the presets, and watches for keyboards you plug in later. A press counts only with exactly the chord's own modifiers held, on any keyboard: Super+X never with Alt, Control or Shift, and Alt+D never with Super, Control or Shift. It needs read access to those devices. It skips two synthetic keyboards by name, VOCO's own virtual keyboard and the device another tool's ydotoold creates, so their keys never count as the shortcut or a held modifier.

facts.title: When nothing hears the shortcut
facts.text: If no keyboard is readable and neither the GNOME companion nor the IBus source takes the preset, the shortcut does nothing at all. 20 seconds after the keyboard reader starts, VOCO says "Your shortcut can't reach VOCO yet" once and names the fix, such as enabling the VOCO panel or assigning voco --toggle to a shortcut.

facts.title: The snap's shortcut on GNOME
facts.text: The snap reads no keyboards. On GNOME Wayland its shortcut is an entry named VOCO in GNOME's own custom keyboard shortcuts, with your shortcut in GTK's spelling, such as <Super>x for Super+X. GNOME's keyboard shortcuts ask nobody, so setup adds the entry by itself on its last screen, and Done waits until GNOME holds it. A saved change of shortcut, from Settings or the tray's presets, moves the entry first. If a GNOME window shortcut or another custom shortcut already uses the keys, VOCO names it and changes nothing. GNOME Settings, under Keyboard, can change the entry's keys too: once setup is complete VOCO saves the keys GNOME holds as its own shortcut, so its labels name the keys GNOME listens for. A start adds no entry, except once where an earlier VOCO's setup left none, so one you removed in GNOME Settings stays removed. GNOME's schema for those keys isn't in the snap's runtime, so the snap carries one with the same IDs, paths and types.

facts.title: A held chord repeats
facts.text: The entry's command calls the running VOCO's Toggle over D-Bus with dbus-send, which takes a few milliseconds, and only where that fails launches /snap/bin/voco --toggle, which takes about 150 ms. GNOME runs the command for the press and again for each repeat while the chord is held, about every 30 ms once the keyboard's repeat delay has passed, and reports no release of either key. VOCO reads that delay and the repeat interval once from GNOME's keyboard settings, and takes 500 ms and 30 ms when it can't. A call is a repeat, and toggles nothing, only at a repeat's time: the first within 100 ms of one repeat delay after a press, the rest sooner than that after the last. Any other is a new press, and VOCO answers every call, so a repeat never falls back to a launch.

facts.title: GNOME 46
facts.text: That timing alone can't tell a second press that comes about one repeat delay after the first. While a dictation's typing session is open, GNOME's keyboard connection says from GNOME 50 whether every modifier was up since the last call, and one that was makes the call a new press whatever its timing, so a dictation stopped half a second after it started still stops. VOCO 2026.0.70 to 2026.0.72 held this shortcut through GNOME's GlobalShortcuts portal on GNOME 48 and later, which shows GNOME's dialog for every new set of keys; VOCO binds nothing through it now. Resetting VOCO's settings removes its entry and only it.

facts.title: Plain status
facts.text: Shortcut help in Settings explains the current route in plain words, for example "VOCO's GNOME panel handles this shortcut.", "GNOME holds this shortcut for VOCO." or "A live synchronized keyboard supports the configured shortcut."

title: Sound becomes numbers.
intro: A microphone measures tiny changes in air pressure. VOCO reads those measurements as a long list of numbers called samples.
story: On Wayland, Rust records through libpulse from PipeWire's Pulse service, which gives each source the identity VOCO needs to select it. It takes 44,100 samples per second on two channels and averages them into one.

On X11, the window records through WebKit with an AudioWorklet. If WebKit offers only the older ScriptProcessor fallback, VOCO can't confirm that it receives every sample. It shows "Dictation won't be typed" and never pastes that recording.
Silence is valid audio, so a long pause never ends a recording. VOCO stops on its own only when capture fails or after ten minutes.

steps.label: Choose a source
steps.detail: Microphone settings list every source and mark monitors of your speakers as (output monitor). VOCO uses the system default only when it is a microphone with a PipeWire identity.

steps.label: Capture
steps.detail: The C layer records 16-bit stereo at 44,100 Hz in 10 ms fragments.

steps.label: Mix to mono
steps.detail: On Wayland, VOCO averages the two channels into one, because the speech model needs one channel.

steps.label: Drain
steps.detail: Rust pumps the stream every 5 ms while recording, and the window collects the samples. If the window stops collecting for 5 seconds, capture ends with "Renderer drain lease expired".

steps.label: Watch health
steps.detail: If capture reports a problem, VOCO ends the recording with an error. At 600 seconds it stops normally, like pressing Stop.

facts.title: No microphone chosen yet
facts.text: VOCO still counts as ready when the system default is a microphone it can record from: the tray reads "VOCO — Ready · microphone checks on first use", and Start dictation chooses that default. Without such a default it reads "VOCO — Microphone setup required". Until you choose one, the window names the microphone System default. VOCO opens no microphone until a recording, a voice test or a Say it check starts.

facts.title: No default microphone
facts.text: When there is no default, or the default is a monitor or has no PipeWire identity, VOCO says "No default microphone is available. Connect a microphone or choose one in Microphone settings."

facts.title: Health checks in WebKit
facts.text: Every 250 ms VOCO checks the WebKit track. It cancels the recording if the track ends, stays muted by the system for 3 seconds or delivers no samples for 5 seconds.

facts.title: The drain lease
facts.text: Only VOCO's main page may drain native capture. If the window stops draining, capture ends after 5 seconds, so a stuck window can't keep the microphone open.

facts.title: A ten-minute limit
facts.text: Both capture paths stop after 600 seconds, and the recording finishes like a normal Stop.

facts.title: The level meter
facts.text: The window computes each level from a batch of samples, the same way on every capture path. The level spans -44 to -12 dB, VOCO sends a new one at most every 40 ms, and a level older than 250 ms reads as silence.

title: Audio on a conveyor belt.
intro: Audio doesn't wait for the end of a sentence. It moves to the speech worker in small packets, like boxes on a conveyor belt.
story: VOCO cuts the audio into packets of one tenth of a second and sends one request to the worker at a time. Each request carries the recording's session name and a number that grows by one.
Each answer holds the whole transcript so far. VOCO compares it with the previous one and passes on only the new ending. Words never change once they move on.
If recognition falls more than three seconds behind, or rewrites words it already gave, VOCO stops transcribing this recording. Words already pasted stay where they are.

steps.label: Collect
steps.detail: The stream gathers round(rate × 0.1) samples, which is 100 ms of audio at any sample rate.

steps.label: Send
steps.detail: Only one request is in flight. Newer packets wait in line.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: Each answer must carry the same session and number as its request, and the append-only mode.

steps.label: Compare
steps.detail: VOCO keeps only text that extends the previous transcript.

steps.label: Paste
steps.detail: The new words go to delivery, each desktop paste ending between two characters that aren't spaces. If a paste is still running, newer words wait and go together.

facts.title: A three-second limit
facts.text: When more than three seconds of audio wait in line, VOCO stops with "Recognition fell more than three seconds behind, so VOCO stopped transcribing."

facts.title: No rewrites
facts.text: If an answer changes earlier words, VOCO stops with "Recognition revised earlier words, so VOCO stopped transcribing." Either way you see "Dictation interrupted", and the words already pasted stay.

facts.title: Three paste outcomes
facts.text: A paste that changes nothing leaves the words pending for the next words, a quiet release or Stop, which retries them 3 times, 250 ms apart. A rejected paste, refused before the clipboard changed, stops typing. An uncertain paste also stops typing, and VOCO never sends those words again.

facts.title: Metadata, not words
facts.text: The queue reports lengths, counts and timings, never the words, and only when VOCO_PERFORMANCE_LOG=1: once Rust answers that logging is off, the window sends no reports. At most 32 reports are in flight; extra ones are dropped and counted, and Rust keeps only the fields it knows.

caution: Append-only is a promise about delivery, not about the model. The model may change its mind, and VOCO stops rather than edit text that is already in an app.

quiz.why: VOCO never edits text it already delivered. A revision breaks the append-only rule, so transcription stops and the pasted words stay as they are.

title: The speech worker has a rulebook.
intro: The speech worker is a separate program. VOCO and the worker follow a short rulebook, one message at a time.
story: VOCO starts one worker when it launches and keeps it warm. The two talk through a pipe: VOCO writes one line of JSON, and the worker answers with one line. The requests are start, push, finish and cancel, and a push carries at most one second of audio.
Every message is checked on both sides. If anything goes wrong, such as a timeout, a mismatched answer or a rejected request, Rust drops the worker.
A new worker starts only at the next warmup or the next recording. VOCO never sends the same request twice, so no audio is processed twice.

steps.label: Launch
steps.detail: Rust runs /usr/bin/python3 -E -s -B with stream_worker.py. VOCO_STREAM_PYTHON and VOCO_STREAM_WORKER may name other absolute local files. The worker has 30 seconds to load the model and report ready.

steps.label: Start
steps.detail: A start names the session, 1 to 80 characters long, and a number that is 0 or more.

steps.label: Push
steps.detail: Each push carries at most one second of mono audio at 8,000 to 96,000 Hz. The rate stays the same for the whole session, and every value must be a finite number.

steps.label: Answer
steps.detail: The worker answers within 10 seconds. A push returns text only when the transcript changed; a finish always returns the final text.

steps.label: Close
steps.detail: A finish or cancel ends the session. Each request's number must be larger than the last.

facts.title: Bounded messages
facts.text: A request may be at most 4 MiB and an answer at most 1 MiB. Anything larger is refused.

facts.title: Clean output
facts.text: stream_worker.py keeps library messages off the protocol, so only answers travel on the worker's output.

facts.title: Your spelling
facts.text: Each session start carries the saved spelling. spelling.py converts the whole hypothesis with a table of unambiguous VarCon forms and emits only text that can no longer change, so pasting stays append-only. Only lowercase words change, so names stay, and so do words whose spelling depends on meaning.

facts.title: Your words
facts.text: Each start also carries the My words list. mywords.py skips any entry that breaks the list rules: at most 100, each at most four words and 40 characters, and at most three combining marks on a letter or digit. adapters.py hands the rest to NeMo-Speech.cpp as one speech context at a boost of 0.5, and the worker writes each listed occurrence as listed, ignoring case, accents and the spaces inside it. The start carries the taught versions too, what the recognizer wrote when you said a word, up to five for each: the worker writes the word wherever it hears one, and never boosts them. A push holds back any tail that later text could still turn into a listed term or a taught version, and spelling never converts a listed word.

facts.title: No network for the worker
facts.text: Just before Python starts, worker_sandbox.rs marks every descriptor beyond the worker's standard streams close-on-exec, so it inherits no socket of VOCO's, and installs a seccomp filter. Every socket and socket pair, Unix ones included, and io_uring fail with permission denied. If the filter can't be installed, the worker doesn't start. The worker also gets only the environment variables it reads, so nothing tells it where the session bus, the display or an agent socket is.

facts.title: The thread rule
facts.text: The worker uses one less than the processors it may run on, between 1 and 4, to leave room for capture, the compositor and the app you are typing into. NEMO_SPEECH_CPU_THREADS overrides it.

facts.title: No replay
facts.text: If the worker dies during a recording, the next push or finish gets "worker lost". Transcription ends for that recording, and the next recording starts a new worker.

facts.title: A processor it can't run on
facts.text: The native recognizer needs AVX2, FMA and F16C. processor.rs reads the first flags line of /proc/cpuinfo once, and when one of them is missing, no worker ever starts: Rust refuses every request with the installer's words, such as "VOCO's speech recognition needs a processor with AVX2, FMA and F16C; this one lacks F16C. In a virtual machine, pass the host CPU through." At startup VOCO shows "Processor not supported" and the tray reads "VOCO — Processor not supported". The window asks the same question before a recording, so a start is refused before any microphone opens. A file without a flags line, as on another architecture, lacks nothing.

facts.title: Private diagnostics
facts.text: When the worker rejects a request, its answer names only the error type after "stream request rejected: ". It never contains audio or text.

title: How the model guesses words.
intro: A speech model doesn't look words up. It makes a careful guess from patterns it learned, and the guess grows as you speak.
story: VOCO uses NVIDIA Nemotron Speech Streaming, an English model with 0.6 billion parameters, stored at 8-bit precision in a GGUF file. It runs on the processor through NeMo-Speech.cpp and needs no graphics card.
The model is built for streaming. It listens in short chunks and keeps a growing guess of the transcript, with punctuation.
Before loading, the worker checks the file's SHA-256 fingerprint. If it doesn't match the pinned value, the worker refuses to start.

steps.label: Verify
steps.detail: The worker computes the model file's SHA-256 and compares it with the pinned value. A mismatch stops the worker before the model loads.

steps.label: Load
steps.detail: The recognizer loads with its right-context setting at 6, 560 ms of audio after the current moment. VOCO_NEMOTRON_CONTEXT accepts 0, 1 or 6, which are 80, 160 or 560 ms; anything else stops the worker.

steps.label: Warm up
steps.detail: Before the first recording, the worker runs one second of zeros at 16,000 Hz through the recognizer.

steps.label: Gate
steps.detail: Long runs of exact digital zeros are skipped. The gate keeps 640 ms before sound and 1.5 seconds after it.

steps.label: Transcribe
steps.detail: The recognizer returns its finished text joined with its latest partial guess.

facts.title: A pinned build
facts.text: NATIVE-BUILD.json records the NeMo-Speech.cpp and ggml revisions and the patch digests. The build targets generic x86-64 with AVX, AVX2, FMA and F16C, and leaves AVX-512, AMX and OpenMP off. That sets the processor VOCO needs: on one that lacks AVX2, FMA or F16C, VOCO starts no worker at all.

facts.title: Two small patches
facts.text: One patch lets the first chunk start without waiting for another 90 ms of audio. The other runs 1 to 16 threads in a pool that sleeps between steps instead of spinning.

facts.title: Fewer, larger frames
facts.text: When the gate releases audio it held back, the worker joins those packets into frames of at most one second, without changing any samples.

facts.title: Original samples
facts.text: The recognizer always receives the original samples at the capture rate, and each push names that rate.

facts.title: The tokenizer inside
facts.text: NVIDIA's GGUF holds the decoder's vocabulary but not the SentencePiece tokenizer the recognizer needs to turn phrases into the model's pieces. VOCO's copy adds that tokenizer from NVIDIA's checkpoint as one metadata entry. Every weight and every other entry stays as NVIDIA published it, and the pinned fingerprint is that of the result.

facts.title: Punctuation comes with the next word
facts.text: Measured on public speech, the recognizer usually writes a comma or full stop only once it hears the next word, so at a pause its text rarely ends in one. In the study's development set, today's recognizer gave 62.7% of pauses between sentences a sentence end, so where you pause the full stop can come a word late or not at all. The worker changes recognized text only for spelling and My words, so VOCO adds no full stop of its own where you pause.

facts.title: Turning the gate off
facts.text: VOCO_SILENCE_GATE=off disables the gate. The default mode, zero, treats a packet as quiet only when every sample is exactly zero. Any other value stops the worker before the model loads.

The bridge into NeMo-Speech.cpp.

quiz.question: Someone replaces the model file with a different one. What happens?
answers: The worker refuses it because the fingerprint doesn't match
VOCO downloads a fresh copy
The worker loads it and transcribes as usual
quiz.why: The worker compares the file's SHA-256 with the pinned value before loading. VOCO never downloads models, so a mismatch stops the worker.

title: Words meet the cursor.
intro: The last step puts words into another app. VOCO does it the way you would: copy, then paste.
story: insertion.rs pastes one group of words at a time. It puts the words on the clipboard, then presses Shift+Insert. In the code's words, "Shift+Insert is the paste key shared by GTK, Qt, Chromium, Firefox, Electron and terminal emulators."

Terminals paste the PRIMARY selection instead of the clipboard, so VOCO fills both. Each live paste ends between two characters that aren't spaces, so its spaces travel inside it. Two spaces go alone: the one before the next words after a quiet release, and the one Stop adds after a finished sentence. Before each paste VOCO checks the helper programs and, on Wayland, access to its own virtual keyboard, or in the snap its typing session with GNOME, and it waits for you to release the shortcut's keys.
An optional Chromium extension offers a second route. In a tab where you enable it, VOCO inserts words at the caret of one plain text field, and the extension confirms each insert with a receipt.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: The text must be 1 to 100,000 bytes and the helpers ready. On Wayland this session must be the active one, and VOCO's own virtual keyboard must exist unless the GNOME companion will press the keys. In the snap without the companion, GNOME's typing session must be open.

steps.label: Clean
steps.detail: Control characters, including newlines and tabs, become spaces, so a terminal never receives Enter.

steps.label: Settle
steps.detail: VOCO lets the app read the previous paste first. Where xclip copies on GNOME Wayland, it watches for that read, for up to 300 ms after the Insert press; elsewhere, and whenever it can't tell, it waits until 150 ms after the previous paste's keys.

steps.label: Copy
steps.detail: The words go to CLIPBOARD and PRIMARY, and a PRIMARY failure only logs a warning. Where xclip copies on GNOME Wayland, PRIMARY goes first, and VOCO waits up to 100 ms for Mutter's read of the new CLIPBOARD, which shows the copy is current.

steps.label: Press
steps.detail: VOCO waits up to 1.5 seconds for the shortcut's modifier keys to be released, and on X11 also while the X server reports Shift, Control, Alt, Super or AltGr held. If they are still down then, it sends no keys. Otherwise it sends Shift+Insert.

facts.title: Every space inside a paste
facts.text: Chromium's address bar strips the spaces at the edges of pasted text, and its rich-text fields turn a space pasted alone into a no-break space. So each live paste ends between two characters that aren't spaces, never inside a letter and its accents, and the last letter waits for the next words. After 0.75 seconds of audio with no new words, the held text goes out on its own. The next words' space is then pasted alone, which the address bar keeps, so a rich-text field gets at most one no-break space for each pause. The final text goes out whole. In the Chromium extension's field each space stays with its words, and a trailing space waits for them.

facts.title: Seeing the app read
facts.text: On GNOME Wayland with DISPLAY set, where xclip copies, each copy runs it in the foreground with -verbose, which reports every request it answers except TARGETS, and keeps the selection until the next copy. Mutter's clipboard manager reads each new CLIPBOARD once. When that read is in by the Insert press, the first answer after the press is the app's read, and the next copy follows at once. A read before the press, during the wait for a young keyboard or the gap after Shift, never counts. A read shows that the app asked for the text, not that the words arrived.

facts.title: Waiting for GNOME's switch
facts.text: A helper reports owning its selection just before its request leaves for the X server, and until the server has it, an app pastes the previous copy. So where xclip copies on GNOME Wayland, VOCO copies PRIMARY first, then CLIPBOARD, and before the keys waits up to 100 ms for Mutter's read of the new CLIPBOARD. Nothing reads PRIMARY that way, so its early copy is a head start, not proof. Without the read in time, the keys go anyway.

facts.title: Keys from inside GNOME Shell
facts.text: On GNOME Wayland, while the companion is attached and the copy GNOME has loaded asks VOCO for work, the companion presses Shift and Insert from inside the Shell with a keyboard of its own, 12 ms apart. It keeps one NextRequest call waiting on VOCO; VOCO answers it with the paste and waits up to 1 second for PasteDone, which carries the moment the Insert press went out. A refusal, because a modifier is held or another paste is in flight, sends no keys, so the words wait, and so does a paste no call took in that second, which VOCO then withdraws. A paste taken but not reported in time is uncertain. Everywhere else, VOCO's own virtual keyboard presses the keys, except in the snap, which can't open /dev/uinput.

facts.title: Keys through GNOME's portal
facts.text: In the snap on GNOME Wayland, when the companion doesn't ask for work, the keys go through GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal, in a session that has only a keyboard. Allow typing, in setup or Settings, shows GNOME's dialog once: turn on Allow Remote Interaction, then choose Share. GNOME returns a restore token, which VOCO keeps beside its settings as remote-desktop-token, so each later session starts without a dialog. Where GNOME's portal also holds the shortcut, the session asks for GNOME's own keyboard connection, which speaks libei's protocol, and from GNOME 50 GNOME reports over it which modifier keys are down. VOCO then sends its keys through that connection; elsewhere it sends them with the portal's NotifyKeyboardKeycode. Either way each paste sends Shift, Insert and their releases, 12 ms apart, and never another key. A failure after Shift went out is uncertain, and VOCO then releases Shift.

facts.title: A session only while you dictate
facts.text: VOCO opens GNOME's typing session when a desktop dictation starts and closes it once VOCO is idle again, after Stop's last paste and space, at a lock, when the window is replaced and at quit. A session still open after two idle checks, 3 seconds apart, closes by itself. While one exists, GNOME shows its orange remote-access icon, and choosing Stop there ends the dictation as Stop does, copying the rest of your words. A paste before the session has started waits up to 400 ms, then changes nothing: "VOCO's typing connection to GNOME isn't ready, so it sent no paste keys." After GNOME's Stop: "GNOME's Stop ended VOCO's typing, so it sent no paste keys."

facts.title: Keys up, through the portal
facts.text: On GNOME 50 the keyboard connection tells VOCO whether Shift, Control, Alt, Super or AltGr is down, and nothing else about the keyboard, so a paste waits only while one really is: keys sent under Super or Alt would make another chord, which pastes nothing. VOCO reads them once more just before Insert, and when one went down under its own Shift it sends no Insert and keeps the words for the next paste. Where GNOME reports no modifiers, as GNOME 46 never does, VOCO's GNOME shortcut tells it only when the chord is pressed and repeated, never when it is let go. With no repeat the letter came up within the repeat delay, and people often let go of Super or Alt a moment after the letter, so a paste waits the repeat delay plus 400 ms after the shortcut's last call, 900 ms by default, or 400 ms when the keyboard doesn't repeat, and as long after a voco --toggle.

facts.title: Three failure outcomes
facts.text: No change: no keys were sent, so the words wait for the next try. Rejected: VOCO refused before touching the clipboard, and typing stops. Uncertain: a helper failed after it started, or the paste keys failed after the copy, so typing stops and VOCO never sends those words again.

facts.title: Checked before recording
facts.text: If a helper is missing, or on Wayland the virtual keyboard can't be used, the recording doesn't start. VOCO shows "Dictation setup incomplete" with the reason. In the snap on GNOME Wayland, until GNOME allows typing or the companion asks for work, the reason reads "VOCO types into your apps through GNOME, which asks you once. Choose Allow typing, then turn on Allow Remote Interaction in GNOME's dialog and choose Share."

facts.title: Checking the originating session
facts.text: A virtual keyboard types into whichever login owns the screen. On Wayland VOCO checks the desktop session it started in before the copy and again just before the keys. That is a graphical login, or the text console a compositor such as Sway was started from, which logind calls tty. When logind reports that session as not active, as after switching to another user, VOCO reports "This desktop session isn't the active local session for VOCO's keyboard, so VOCO sent no paste keys." If logind can't answer, VOCO doesn't block. These checks don't lock the session: switching after the last check can still redirect keys.

facts.title: Nothing while the screen is locked
facts.text: VOCO follows logind's LockedHint for the session it started in. While the screen is locked, a paste fails with "The screen is locked, so VOCO sent no paste keys." and no shortcut starts dictation. Locking the screen during a dictation stops it, and VOCO shows "Dictation stopped" with "VOCO stopped listening when the screen locked." GNOME doesn't end a remote desktop session at the lock, so VOCO closes the snap's typing session itself.

facts.title: VOCO steps aside
facts.text: If VOCO's own window is showing when you start, VOCO hides it instead of recording and shows "VOCO hidden" with "Click where you want the text, then start dictation again."

facts.title: The browser route
facts.text: The Chromium extension works through its toolbar button and Alt+Shift+V. It inserts only into a text area or a text, search, URL or telephone input with a collapsed caret. It skips disabled and read-only fields, fields inside a private or inert area, and fields whose autocomplete asks for a password, a one-time code or payment details. Incognito tabs are refused, and an insert counts only when a matching receipt comes back.

facts.title: The clipboard keeps the words
facts.text: VOCO doesn't restore what the clipboard held before. After dictation, the clipboard holds VOCO's last paste, such as the end of your last word or the space Stop adds after a finished sentence. The helper holding it keeps running, even after VOCO quits, until something else is copied.

One thread that holds every portal request, session and signal, so waiting for GNOME's dialog never blocks GTK's main thread.
Holds a paste for the repeat delay and 400 ms after the snap's GNOME shortcut last called, where GNOME reports no modifiers.
Allow typing, and the snap's shortcut: added by setup itself, with an Add button in Settings.
Tracks the originating desktop session and asks logind whether it is active and locked.
Checks paste readiness before a recording starts.
Hides VOCO's window before dictation into another app.

Typed wrappers for the paste and copy commands.

The native messaging host the extension talks to.
The messages between VOCO and the extension.

caution: Dispatched means the paste keys went out. On GNOME VOCO also sees the app read the clipboard, but only the browser route gets a receipt from the page; for other apps VOCO can't see whether the words arrived.

quiz.question: A paste helper fails after it started. Why doesn't VOCO simply try again?
answers: The keys may already have reached the app, so a retry could type the words twice
Helpers can run only once per recording
VOCO retries silently in the background
quiz.why: After a helper starts, the clipboard or the app may already hold the words. VOCO marks the paste uncertain and never replays it.

title: Stop means finish the work.
intro: Pressing Stop doesn't throw away the end of your sentence. VOCO finishes the work before it goes quiet.
story: When you stop, VOCO flushes the microphone and sends the audio the worker hasn't heard yet, including the last partial packet. Then it asks for the final transcript and pastes the last words, and after a finished sentence, one space.
If some words couldn't be pasted, VOCO copies them to the clipboard and tells you. If even the copy fails, the words wait in Review.
A recognition failure is different. VOCO copies nothing, because the transcript may be missing words, and asks you to check your text field.

steps.label: Flush
steps.detail: On X11 the AudioWorklet must confirm its flush within 80 ms. Otherwise VOCO says "The end of this recording could not be confirmed, so VOCO did not finish it. Try again."

steps.label: Forward the tail
steps.detail: VOCO sends the retained samples the stream hasn't received, then the partial packet.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: The worker returns the final transcript. Words still pending get up to 3 more paste attempts, 250 ms apart.

steps.label: Deliver or copy
steps.detail: Words left over go to CLIPBOARD and PRIMARY, with any space before them, and VOCO shows "Dictation copied to clipboard".

steps.label: Clean up
steps.detail: VOCO clears the audio from memory and deletes the recording's journal entry.

facts.title: A space after a finished sentence
facts.text: When the whole final text went out, with no cancel and no failed or uncertain paste, and it ends with . ? ! or …, perhaps before closing quotes or brackets, Stop pastes one space on its own after it, so your next dictation or typing starts apart. It never does in the Chromium extension's field, the voice test or Say it. If that paste fails, VOCO says nothing and copies nothing, because no words are missing.

facts.title: Typing stopped, listening continues
facts.text: When a paste is rejected or uncertain, VOCO shows "VOCO stopped typing" with "It's still listening. When you stop, VOCO copies the rest of your words to the clipboard."

facts.title: After an uncertain paste
facts.text: The clipboard notice warns: "Some words may already be in the app, so check it first. Then press Shift+Insert or Ctrl+V to paste the rest."

facts.title: When the copy fails
facts.text: VOCO keeps the words in Review and shows "Dictation saved in Review" with "VOCO couldn't paste or copy it. Choose Review in VOCO's menu to copy it." If even that fails, the window shows "VOCO couldn't paste, copy or save this dictation."

facts.title: When recognition fails
facts.text: VOCO shows "Dictation interrupted" with "Some words may be missing. Check your text field before starting again." If no words were recognized yet, the message starts "Nothing was typed." and gives the reason instead. Nothing is copied.

facts.title: Unconfirmed audio is never typed
facts.text: When WebKit offered only the ScriptProcessor fallback, VOCO already showed "Dictation won't be typed". At Stop it clears the audio, and the window shows "VOCO couldn't confirm it received all of your audio, so it didn't type this recording. Try again."

files.why: The Stop sequence, the clipboard copy and every notice.
Forwards the audio the stream hasn't received.
The 80 ms flush confirmation.
Finishes the stream, reports undelivered words and whether all of the final text went out.
Copies leftover words to both selections without sending keys.
Saves words in Review when copying fails.

caution: Stop never replays words as key presses after typing stopped. Words that weren't typed go to the clipboard, or to Review if copying fails.

quiz.question: A paste failed during the recording, but recognition kept going. What does Stop do with the words that weren't typed?
answers: Types them with simulated key presses
Copies them to the clipboard and tells you to paste them
Discards them
quiz.why: Stop never replays words as key presses. It copies the rest to CLIPBOARD and PRIMARY and shows "Dictation copied to clipboard", so you choose where to paste.

title: When something goes wrong.
intro: Computers crash sometimes. VOCO keeps a small private note of what you said, so a crash doesn't lose your words.
story: While you dictate, VOCO writes the transcript, and only the transcript, to a journal on disk. A normal finish deletes the entry, and so do Quit and a clean shutdown signal.
If VOCO exits unexpectedly, the entry stays. At the next start VOCO moves it to Review, where it waits for you.
Review opens only when you choose it from VOCO's menu. You can copy each transcript or discard it, and Review never pastes anything by itself.

steps.label: Record
steps.detail: Each new result updates the recording's entry. An entry larger than 256 KiB is refused.

steps.label: Finish
steps.detail: A normal finish deletes the entry.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: At the next start, an unfinished entry moves to Review. If only the window reloads, it moves at once.

steps.label: Keep five
steps.detail: Review keeps up to five entries and removes the oldest.

steps.label: Choose
steps.detail: Copy transcript puts the text on the clipboard. Discard first asks "Discard this transcript?" and offers Keep or Discard transcript.

facts.title: Owner-only files
facts.text: The journal lives in $XDG_STATE_HOME/voco/crash-recovery, or ~/.local/state/voco/crash-recovery when that variable is unset, empty or relative. Only your user can read it.

facts.title: When the journal is unavailable
facts.text: Dictation still works. VOCO shows "Crash recovery unavailable" with "Dictation continues, but VOCO can't recover it if VOCO exits unexpectedly."

facts.title: Clean exits clean up
facts.text: Quit VOCO, SIGINT and SIGTERM delete the active entry, because those exits are chosen, not crashes.

facts.title: When the window crashes
facts.text: WebKit runs VOCO's window in a process of its own. If that process crashes, VOCO loads the window again, its unfinished entry moves to Review, and VOCO shows "Dictation interrupted" if you were dictating. If it crashes again after three reloads in five minutes, VOCO leaves it closed and shows "VOCO stopped working".

facts.title: Review is explicit
facts.text: Each entry is "Kept until you discard it." VOCO never opens, pastes or retries recovered text for you.

facts.title: Cleanup failures
facts.text: If temporary text can't be deleted, VOCO says "Temporary dictation text could not be deleted. VOCO will retry cleanup before the next recording."

files.why: The owner-only journal, its size bound and Review's five entries.
Loads the window again when its web process crashes, at most three times in five minutes.
The window's side of the journal.
The Review screen: copy or discard.
Writes and finishes the journal during a recording.
Tests for journal updates and cleanup.
The menu item that opens Review.

caution: Quitting VOCO while you dictate deletes the unfinished entry. Review protects against crashes, not against choosing Quit.

quiz.question: VOCO crashes in the middle of a recording. What happens to the words you said?
answers: They are pasted automatically at the next start
They are lost, because the journal is deleted
They wait in Review until you open it from VOCO's menu
quiz.why: An unexpected exit leaves the journal entry in place. At the next start VOCO moves it to Review, which opens only when you choose it and never pastes by itself.

title: A small interface, clear ownership.
intro: VOCO has few settings, and one part owns them. That keeps the file simple and safe.
story: VOCO keeps its settings in one file, and Rust owns it. The window sends small changes, called patches, and Rust refuses fields it doesn't know and null values.
Fields from older versions are ignored and dropped at the next save. If VOCO can't read the file, it never overwrites it. Dictation pauses, and a recovery panel offers three ways out.
Each save leaves a copy beside the file, so settings an earlier VOCO drops come back at the next start, unless a reset happened in between. Only Reset keeps a backup of the old file.

steps.label: Load
steps.detail: Rust reads $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/voco/config.json and takes any setting it lacks from config.json.last, unless a reset renamed the file since that copy was saved.

steps.label: Migrate
steps.detail: If that file doesn't exist, VOCO copies $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/voice/config.json when present.

steps.label: Patch
steps.detail: The window sends only the fields that changed. Unknown fields and null values are refused.

steps.label: Save
steps.detail: Rust writes the file atomically, then the same settings to config.json.last, keeping any that a later VOCO left there. The folder is 0700 and the files 0600, so only you can read them.

steps.label: Recover
steps.detail: When the file can't be read, the recovery panel offers Retry loading settings, Open config directory and Reset to defaults.

facts.title: Ten fields
facts.text: hotkey, which defaults to Super+X; selectedMic; onboardingCompleted; startAtLogin, which defaults to true; updateChannel; automaticUpdateChecks, which defaults to true; englishSpelling, unset until chosen, which means British; myWords, empty until you add a word; myWordsHeard, the versions VOCO learned when you said a word; and installChannel.

facts.title: Update checks
facts.text: VOCO checks after startup and when you change the update channel, unless Update checks is set to Only when I choose. It reuses an answer younger than 6 hours, and otherwise asks GitHub for the 12 newest releases, with a 15-second timeout. Check for updates in Settings always asks. The snap never checks: Settings shows its version and "The Snap Store keeps VOCO up to date."

facts.title: A notice, then your choice
facts.text: When a newer release exists, VOCO shows an "Update available" notification once for that release: "Open VOCO's Settings, then Updates, to install it." A check only reads. Nothing downloads or installs until you choose Install update.

facts.title: Install update
facts.text: The .deb and the RPM have it; the snap and a source build don't. VOCO downloads voco_checksums.txt, its signature and the one package for this system from that release on GitHub into a private folder, following at most three redirects and only to release-assets.githubusercontent.com. It checks the signature with gpgv against the release key it carries, then the package's SHA-256, name, version and architecture. A failure installs nothing, deletes the download and says why.

facts.title: The root helper
facts.text: Only pkexec runs /usr/libexec/voco-update-helper, through a polkit action that always asks for an administrator's password. It sets its own umask, 022, because pkexec keeps the caller's, so nothing it creates is writable by your group. It takes just the folder and the version, copies the three files into /var/cache/voco-update, checks them again, refuses a release that isn't newer than the installed one, and runs apt-get install or dnf install on that copy. VOCO then restarts. You can cancel only the download, and from the password prompt until VOCO exits no recording can start.

facts.title: Two channels
facts.text: The default channel ignores pre-releases, and its helper text reads "Recommended for everyday use." Beta includes them: "Beta releases change more often." Drafts are always ignored.

facts.title: Start at login
facts.text: In the packages and the snap, Settings offers Start VOCO when you sign in, under Startup, and it is on until you turn it off; a source build has no switch. On, it reads "VOCO starts without opening a window, ready for your shortcut." Off: "After you sign in, open VOCO from your app launcher before you dictate." Turning it on or off changes the login entry first, so if that fails, the setting and the entry both stay as they were.

facts.title: Installation method
facts.text: installChannel only chooses which update instructions VOCO shows.

facts.title: Reset is confirmed
facts.text: Reset to defaults asks "Reset local settings?" and needs Confirm reset before it replaces the file. It keeps the old file as a recovery backup and deletes config.json.last and the backups of earlier resets. In the snap it also forgets GNOME's permission to type, the restore token in remote-desktop-token, and removes VOCO's entry from GNOME's keyboard shortcuts with its note in gnome-shortcut, so setup asks GNOME to let VOCO type and adds the shortcut again.

facts.title: Back from an earlier version
facts.text: An earlier VOCO rewrites the file without the settings it doesn't know. The next start takes them back from config.json.last, keeping what you changed in the earlier version. A reset in between wins: every VOCO names its backup with the time of the reset, and a backup newer than the copy means nothing comes back. A restored taught version that clashes with the list is dropped, and the log gives only how many.

Keeps GNOME's typing permission beside the settings, and forgets it at Reset.
The settings window, including the update channel and the login switch.
Keeps the login entry in step with the setting.
Tells the window when the Snap Store updates VOCO, so it never checks.
The three ways out when settings can't load.
Asks GitHub for releases and filters them by channel.
Decides when to check and when to reuse the cached answer.
Runs Install update: download, verify, the helper, then the restart.
Downloads a release's three files, only from GitHub's release assets.
Checks the signature, the checksum and the package's identity.
The root helper that installs a verified release.

The window that shows Download, Verify, Install and Restart.

caution: Settings stay on this computer. VOCO has no account and syncs nothing.

Rust saves it for later versions

quiz.why: Rust owns the file and accepts only the fields it knows. A patch with an unknown field is refused, so nothing unexpected reaches the file.

title: One app, several Linux paths.
intro: A Linux desktop is made of many parts. VOCO fits into them with a few small, private pieces.
story: Only one copy of VOCO runs per login. Launching it again brings the running copy forward and never starts a recording.
Other programs reach VOCO through private sockets that check the caller's user ID. Notifications go through D-Bus, the desktop's message bus.

On Wayland, VOCO presses the paste keys through its own virtual keyboard, or on GNOME through the companion once it asks VOCO for work. A udev rule in the package lets the person at the computer use /dev/uinput, so there is no service, daemon or group to set up. The snap can't open /dev/uinput, so on GNOME Wayland it types through the companion when it asks for work, and otherwise through GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal.

steps.label: Lock
steps.detail: instance.lock in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/voco makes sure only one copy runs.

steps.label: Activate
steps.detail: A second launch connects to voco-activate.sock and asks the running copy to show itself, waiting at most 2 seconds.

steps.label: Trigger
steps.detail: voco.sock and voice.sock sit in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or in a private voco-<uid> folder in the temporary directory when that variable is unset. The sockets are 0600, and a connection is the request.

steps.label: Notify
steps.detail: Notifications go through D-Bus with a 3-second timeout.

steps.label: Keyboard
steps.detail: On Wayland, VOCO creates its virtual keyboard at startup and keeps it until it quits.

facts.title: Command-line options
facts.text: voco accepts --toggle, --check-desktop-input, --check-panel, --setup-panel, --version and --help. Unknown arguments exit with code 2.

facts.title: A launcher click opens VOCO
facts.text: When VOCO's own launcher starts it, GIO names VOCO.desktop and this process, so VOCO shows its popover as it would for a second launch. A start from a terminal or a login autostart stays in the tray.

facts.title: Starting at login
facts.text: Once setup is complete, and while Start VOCO when you sign in is on, VOCO keeps one entry, voco-login.desktop, in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/autostart, and removes it otherwise. It brings the entry in step at startup and after every settings save, and never writes through a link or into another user's file. TryExec=voco makes the session skip the entry once the package is gone. In the snap, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME is the snap's own folder, and the recipe's autostart key tells snapd to start VOCO from that entry. A login start stays in the tray, and a source build keeps no entry.

facts.title: A hidden window
facts.text: With native capture VOCO really hides its window. On X11, where WebKit records, VOCO instead shrinks the window to 1 by 1 pixel and moves it off-screen.

facts.title: Checking input
facts.text: voco --check-desktop-input checks the paste prerequisites without launching VOCO or sending keys: the clipboard helper, xdotool on X11, and on Wayland that /dev/uinput opens for reading and writing. In the snap on GNOME Wayland it instead passes when the running VOCO answers through CompanionAsking that the companion asks it for work, since only that VOCO knows, or when GNOME's typing permission is saved. It exits with code 1 when something is missing.

facts.title: Access from a udev rule
facts.text: 70-voco-uinput.rules tags /dev/uinput with uaccess, so logind gives the user of the active local session access through an ACL that follows seat changes. voco-uinput.conf loads the uinput module at boot.

facts.title: A leftover service
facts.text: At a Wayland start, VOCO removes a leftover link to voco-ydotoold.service from this login's systemd folder, but only if the link points at /usr/lib/systemd/user/voco-ydotoold.service and that file no longer exists. Then it stops the unit and reloads the user manager, off the startup path.

facts.title: Two packages and a snap, one tree
facts.text: The Debian package depends on xclip, xdotool and wl-clipboard, among others, and recommends nothing. The Fedora RPM is built from the same staged files and requires the same packages under their Fedora names. The snap carries those files too, except what strict confinement can't use.

facts.title: The snap
facts.text: When snapd names it voco, VOCO knows it runs as its snap and leaves out the virtual keyboard, the keyboard reader, the IBus listener and the update check. On GNOME Wayland the companion types for it once it asks for work, and otherwise GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal does, after you allow it once: "VOCO types into your apps through GNOME, which asks you once. Choose Allow typing, then turn on Allow Remote Interaction in GNOME's dialog and choose Share." On other Wayland desktops Start is refused: "The VOCO snap types only on GNOME and in X11 sessions. On this desktop, install VOCO's .deb or RPM from its GitHub releases instead." X11 keeps xdotool.

facts.title: Connections the snap needs
facts.text: Where its plugs aren't connected, the snap says how to connect them. Before each recording it asks snapctl whether audio-record is connected: "The VOCO snap can't use the microphone yet. Allow it in Settings, under Apps, then VOCO, or run snap connect voco:audio-record. Then try again." PipeWire settles what a snap may record when it connects, so native capture connects only once the plug is, and the same VOCO then records. WebKit, which captures on X11, lists its microphones once, so there VOCO asks to be restarted. logind refuses the snap until login-session-observe is connected, and while it does, the paste check asks snapctl about the plug before it asks logind again.

title: Draw the trust boundaries.
intro: Privacy is easier to check when you can see where each piece of data goes. VOCO keeps the map short.
story: Audio stays in memory while you record and is cleared when the recording ends. It travels to the worker over a private pipe, never over the network.
Text lives briefly in the crash journal and on the clipboard. The window may connect only to VOCO itself and GitHub's release API.
Logs are off by default. When you turn them on, they hold metadata such as lengths and timings, never your words or audio.

steps.detail: VOCO's sockets are owner-only, and the trigger, activation, IBus and browser sockets check the caller's user ID through one shared helper.

steps.label: Files

facts.title: Debug audio
facts.text: Saving audio needs three variables, VOCO_DEV_NATIVE_CAPTURE, VOCO_DEBUG_CAPTURE_AUDIO and VOCO_DEBUG_NATIVE_CAPTURE, all set to exactly 1. Then VOCO writes one owner-only bundle in $XDG_STATE_HOME/voco/debug-native-captures after the recording.

facts.title: The clipboard is shared
facts.text: Other apps can read the clipboard. VOCO pastes through it and doesn't restore what it held before.

facts.title: No shell access
facts.text: The window has no shell plugin. Its permissions are Tauri's core defaults and a list of window controls, so it can't register global shortcuts either.

facts.title: Browser limits
facts.text: The Chromium extension refuses incognito tabs, skips password, one-time-code and payment fields, and works only in tabs where you enable it.

facts.title: Paste keys for one person
facts.text: The package's uaccess rule gives /dev/uinput to the user of the active local session alone, with no group, daemon or socket. VOCO's keyboard can press only Shift and Insert, and so can the GNOME companion's, which answers only the attached VOCO. The snap's typing session with GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal has only a keyboard, sends only Shift and Insert, and exists only while you dictate, with GNOME's orange remote-access icon showing. Before copying and before sending keys, VOCO checks its originating session. An inactive or locked result stops the paste; an unavailable result permits it. A switch after the check can still redirect keys.

facts.title: The snap's sandbox
facts.text: The snap plugs no network, home folder or input device, so it can't reach the internet, read your home folder outside its own folders or open /dev/uinput. The Snap Store updates it. On the session bus it owns com.sergiopesch.voco.Panel, a name under the maintainer's own domain, through a dbus slot, which lets it answer GNOME Shell but never call it.

facts.title: Same user, not same program
facts.text: The sockets keep out other users. They are not a boundary against a compromised program that runs as you.

facts.title: Measured, not only promised
facts.text: check-privacy.sh runs a release build twice in a container and dictates a public clip each time. With update checks off and no network, no process may connect, send or bind to an internet address, or ask DNS anything. With them on, only api.github.com may be resolved and reached, and the speech worker reaches nothing. In both, a microphone stream exists only while dictation runs.

title: Measure the right stopwatch.
intro: A time is only useful when you know where the stopwatch starts and stops. VOCO's measurements always say which clock they use.
story: Performance logging is off until you turn it on. Then VOCO and the worker record timings and resource use, never words or audio.
report-performance.py summarizes the log with counts, medians, 95th percentiles and maximums, and never scores what it didn't measure.
A replay script feeds pinned public speech to the real worker, so one machine can be measured again under the same conditions.

facts.title: Logging never blocks speech
facts.text: Log records wait in a queue of 256. When it is full, VOCO drops the record and counts it rather than slow dictation.

facts.title: Named failures
facts.text: Queue failures are logged by name, such as backlog_limit and prefix_revision, with a hashed session instead of the session itself.

facts.title: Threads
facts.text: By default the worker uses at most 4 threads, one less than the processors it may use.

facts.title: Know what is measured
facts.text: Each quality record names its clock_domain and counts samples at queue_ingress, where audio enters the queue. The replay measures the worker's process boundary, not capture, the receiving app or the screen.

facts.title: Reads, not proof
facts.text: Each paste's record says which selection the app read and how many milliseconds after the Insert press, that nothing read it within 300 ms, or that the helpers couldn't tell, as they can only where xclip copies on GNOME Wayland. A read shows that the app asked for the text, not that the words arrived.

facts.title: Which keyboard typed
facts.text: Each paste's record also names the keyboard that sent its keys: companion, uinput, portal or xdotool. report-dictation-quality-events.py counts them for each session, so timings can be compared by keyboard.

facts.title: Descriptive statistics
facts.text: Percentiles use the nearest-rank method and keep their sample counts. A few runs describe those runs, nothing more.

facts.text: The Wayland delivery suites give their private session /dev/uinput but no /dev/input. facts.text: On each Shell it runs, the companion suite pastes into a GTK field 200 times through the companion and 200 times through Mutter's RemoteDesktop API, taking turns. facts.title: GNOME 50 and 51, headless

facts.title: The snap's portals
facts.text: GNOME 50 Portals runs a headless GNOME Shell 50 with XWayland, PipeWire, the real xdg-desktop-portal, its GNOME backend and GNOME's media keys daemon, and answers GNOME's dialog over AT-SPI. VOCO's typing and shortcut code runs as the snap through a test fixture. Without permission a paste is refused before the copy. Allow typing shows GNOME's dialog once, and later dictations restore it without one. Ten pastes land exactly in a GTK field on Wayland and ten under XWayland, the remote-access icon's Stop ends the dictation with no key after it, and an idle session closes by itself. VOCO's shortcut joins GNOME's keyboard shortcuts with no dialog, and Super+X then toggles through GNOME's daemon and the entry's real command and never reaches the field. With GNOME's keyboard connection a paste under the held chord goes out once Super is up, one after Super was let go first waits for nothing, one under Control alone waits for its release, and a modifier pressed under VOCO's own Shift gets no Insert. A chord held past the repeat delay runs the command for every repeat and toggles once, and a press half a second after the last, during a dictation, toggles. With the connection turned off the same pastes wait the repeat delay plus 400 ms after the shortcut's last call. A change of shortcut moves the entry at once, three times over, keys another shortcut uses are refused, and a reset removes VOCO's entry and only it.

title: How source becomes an app.
intro: Shipping turns source code into a package someone can trust. Each step leaves proof that the next step can check.
story: A release starts from a signed tag on a commit that already passed CI on master. The build runs from a clean tree, and its timestamps come from the last commit.
The build adds the speech runtime and model to a Debian package, builds a Fedora RPM from the same staged files, checks both and signs the checksums.
The installer runs the chain backwards. It checks the signature, then the checksum, and only then installs.

title: Borrowed code needs care.
intro: VOCO builds on libraries other people wrote. A few need small fixes, so VOCO keeps patched copies and checks them.

Each patch is small and has one reason: in glib a security fix, in global-hotkey an X11 shortcut actor that waits for events instead of polling, and in tray-icon icons that stay valid while VOCO runs. The package carries each one's licenses and patch notes.
Scripts check each patched copy against its recorded origin, so a later update can't quietly bring back the unpatched code.

title: A microphone in the top bar.
intro: On GNOME, VOCO can live in the top bar near the clock, with bars that move while you speak.
story: The optional companion for GNOME 46, 48, 50 and 51 shows VOCO's microphone in the top bar. While you dictate, a seven-bar meter opens on its left when there is room beside the clock.

The installer runs voco --setup-panel, and VOCO's setup and Help offer Enable live panel. Enabling adds only this extension, may need you to sign out and back in, and never restarts the Shell. The package alone never enables it, and voco --check-panel changes nothing. The snap can't enable extensions and types without the companion, so its setup never asks for it, and Help offers Get the VOCO panel, which opens the companion's page on extensions.gnome.org.

Once the companion attaches, VOCO hides its tray icon. On Wayland the companion grabs the configured preset, Super+X, Alt+D or Alt+Shift+D, inside the Shell, so other apps never see the shortcut, and presses VOCO's paste keys.

steps.label: Enable
steps.detail: voco --setup-panel or Enable live panel turns on this one extension for your user.

steps.label: Attach
steps.detail: The companion calls Attach over D-Bus. VOCO accepts it only from the process that owns org.gnome.Shell, then hides the tray icon. A refused Attach is tried again 2 seconds later.

steps.label: Poll
steps.detail: The companion asks for VOCO's state every 50 ms while recording and every 1500 ms otherwise.

steps.label: Grab
steps.detail: On Wayland it grabs the configured preset and renews a 2.5-second lease about once a second.

steps.label: Release
steps.detail: If GetState stops arriving for more than 5 seconds, or the companion calls Detach, VOCO drops the lease and shows the tray icon again.

facts.title: The menu
facts.text: A primary click stops dictation, or opens VOCO when nothing can be stopped. Other mouse buttons, the Menu key and Shift+F10 open a menu with Settings, Review, Stop dictation and Quit VOCO. Quit is greyed out while VOCO dictates, and the companion offers it only to a VOCO that sends canQuit. Stop names the recording it ends, so the companion offers it only once VOCO's state carries that recording's session.

facts.title: Motion
facts.text: Bars grow in 45 ms and shrink in 100 ms. While VOCO processes, the bars hold at 0.35 and pulse over 700 ms, each bar 40 ms after the last. The meter opens in 220 ms. When the Shell's animations are off, by the desktop's setting or while the Shell holds them back, every change happens at once and nothing pulses.

facts.title: The bar formula
facts.text: Each bar's height is 0.15 + 0.85 × level × weight, with weights 0.35, 0.65, 0.9, 1, 0.8, 0.55 and 0.3 from left to right.

facts.title: Fresh levels only
facts.text: A level older than 250 ms reads as silence, so the bars never freeze on an old value.

facts.title: One job per file
facts.text: extension.js only creates the companion when GNOME enables it and destroys it when GNOME disables it. companion.js speaks VOCO's protocol: Attach, the GetState poll and the one waiting NextRequest. indicator.js draws the pill, the meter and the menu, paster.js types the paste keys, shortcut.js holds the grab and version.js reads the Shell's major version. Each class removes what it created.

facts.title: No late replies
facts.text: The companion keeps its poll, request and retry timeouts by name, and scheduling one removes the one it replaces. Every call of an attachment carries one Gio.Cancellable, which is cancelled and replaced when the attachment ends, so no late reply is read. The grab is one object, and a reply about a grab no longer held never acts on a newer one.

facts.title: Keys released
facts.text: When VOCO can't read the keyboards, it asks the companion whether the shortcut's keys are up before a Wayland paste, and waits at most 150 ms for its ModifiersState report.

facts.title: VOCO never calls the Shell
facts.text: A strict snap may answer GNOME Shell but never call it, so the companion asks VOCO for work, on com.sergiopesch.voco.Panel. A copy from before companion version 19 speaks only the old name, org.voco.Panel, and never reaches this VOCO. It keeps one NextRequest call waiting, for up to 30 seconds, and calls again as soon as VOCO answers: with a paste, a modifier check, a change of state, or idle after 20 seconds.

facts.title: Paste keys from the Shell
facts.text: For a paste, the companion presses Shift and Insert with one virtual keyboard per enable, 12 ms apart, then reports PasteDone with the time the Insert press went out. VOCO takes a report only from the attached Shell and only for its open request. The companion refuses with ModifiersHeld while a modifier is held and with Busy while another paste is in flight. Disabled during a paste, it releases the keys it holds and reports Disabled, which VOCO treats as uncertain, and GNOME disables it at the lock screen.

facts.title: Setup messages
facts.text: Active: "Live panel bars and Stop are active." Disabled: "Enable live microphone bars and the VOCO menu in your top panel." After enabling: "Panel enabled. Sign out and back in to load it; saving your work first is recommended." After an update, including a copy the Shell marked out of date at login: "Panel update installed. Save your work, then sign out and back in to load the current panel and shortcut." GNOME loads a copy in your own extensions folder in place of the package's, so setup reports one that isn't the current version as blocked, and never removes it. Its message names the folder after "Another copy of the VOCO panel, in" and ends "Remove that folder, then save your work and sign out and back in."

facts.title: The panel and the snap
facts.text: The snap's VOCO can't enable extensions, and it types without the companion, so the panel is optional there. On GNOME Wayland Help says "Optional: the VOCO panel adds live microphone bars and Stop to your top bar, and VOCO then types without GNOME's orange icon. Get it from extensions.gnome.org." On X11, where the snap types with xdotool, the note has no clause about the orange icon. Once the companion attaches and asks for work, it types for the snap instead of GNOME's portal, and setup skips its typing step. GNOME's shortcut steps aside only while the companion's lease holds the saved chord, because a companion before version 23 grabs only Alt chords, so with Super+X GNOME's shortcut is still needed. Setup's own check answers once, so when the once-a-second diagnostics turn ready, as when the companion attaches, setup checks again by itself.

facts.title: Other desktops
facts.text: On other GNOME versions: "The VOCO panel supports GNOME 46, 48, 50 and 51. Dictation still works, but without the panel the focused app also receives the shortcut. To avoid that, choose another shortcut in VOCO and configure it in your desktop to run voco --toggle." On other desktops: "Use the VOCO tray menu for status and Stop. Labels depend on your desktop."

facts.title: From GNOME 50
facts.text: GNOME 50 and 51 have no Meta.is_wayland_compositor, so the companion treats a Shell without it as Wayland. Their panel button opens the menu from a click gesture, so the companion leaves primary presses and touches to the pill, and a primary click still stops dictation or opens VOCO.

facts.title: No icon at all
facts.text: The tray icon needs a tray host, on GNOME an AppIndicator extension, which Debian and Fedora don't turn on. If 20 seconds after startup the companion isn't attached and no tray host owns org.kde.StatusNotifierWatcher, VOCO says "VOCO has no icon in the top bar" once. On GNOME it adds "Open VOCO from the app menu, choose Enable live panel in Help, then sign out and back in." and in the snap "Open VOCO from the app menu and choose Get the VOCO panel in Help."

facts.title: The tray fallback
facts.text: Without the companion, the tray shows 3 state icons and, while you dictate, animates 64 meter frames every 90 ms.

facts.title: The check cache
facts.text: VOCO reuses a panel check for 20 seconds, or for 2 seconds after a failed check.

facts.title: Before the companion loads
facts.text: A running Shell finds a companion the package just installed only at the next login, and keeps running an older copy it already loaded until then. A first install from extensions.gnome.org, as the snap's Help offers, loads at once. While the focused app also gets the shortcut, setup's last step leads with VOCO's note on what the shortcut does there and the fix, and the dictation instruction follows it. The note comes from the once-a-second diagnostics, so it changes when you enable the panel.

title: Each desktop, its own helpers.
intro: Linux desktops differ in how programs may read keys and send them. VOCO picks a helper for each job from the session it runs in.
story: VOCO reads XDG_SESSION_TYPE, WAYLAND_DISPLAY and DISPLAY. If XDG_SESSION_TYPE says wayland, VOCO takes the Wayland path. If it says x11, VOCO takes X11 even when WAYLAND_DISPLAY is set. When XDG_SESSION_TYPE is tty, unset or empty, WAYLAND_DISPLAY chooses Wayland and DISPLAY alone chooses X11; neither variable means no desktop session.

On Wayland, keys go through VOCO's own virtual keyboard, a uinput device named VOCO virtual keyboard, or on GNOME through the companion's keyboard inside the Shell once it asks VOCO for work. The snap, which can't open /dev/uinput, types on GNOME Wayland through GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal when the companion doesn't. On GNOME with an X display, xclip sets the clipboard through XWayland: GNOME lacks the wlroots data-control protocol, wl-copy's temporary focus surface can stall, and XWayland bridges the clipboard without taking focus. Other Wayland desktops use wl-copy.
On X11, xdotool sends the keys and xclip sets the clipboard. The table below shows each combination.

steps.label: Detect
steps.detail: XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland selects Wayland. XDG_SESSION_TYPE=x11 selects X11 even when WAYLAND_DISPLAY is set. When XDG_SESSION_TYPE is tty, unset or empty, WAYLAND_DISPLAY chooses Wayland and DISPLAY alone chooses X11.

steps.label: Shortcut
steps.detail: On X11 VOCO grabs the chord. On Wayland the GNOME companion grabs it, or VOCO reads the keyboards for the three presets. The snap on GNOME Wayland asks GNOME to hold it.

steps.label: Keys
steps.detail: On Wayland the GNOME companion presses Shift+Insert once it asks for work, and VOCO's virtual keyboard otherwise, or in the snap GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal. X11 uses xdotool.

steps.label: Clipboard
steps.detail: xclip on X11 and on GNOME with DISPLAY set, wl-copy on other Wayland sessions.

steps.label: Paste
steps.detail: Every path ends with Shift+Insert into the focused app.

facts.title: One keyboard for the whole run
facts.text: VOCO creates the keyboard at startup and keeps it until it quits, never one per paste. The compositor adds a new device late and could miss its first keys, so a keyboard younger than 500 ms waits before it types. When VOCO exits, the kernel removes the device and releases any key it held.

facts.title: Two keys, one at a time
facts.text: The keyboard declares only Shift and Insert. Each press and release goes out in its own report, 12 ms apart, so every toolkit sees the chord in order and a paste still takes under 100 ms.

facts.title: Access without a helper
facts.text: The package's udev rule gives the user of the active local session access to /dev/uinput. To check it, voco --check-desktop-input only opens /dev/uinput; it never creates the device or sends keys. Without access it says "VOCO can't open /dev/uinput, so it can't send the paste keys. Sign out and back in once after installing VOCO; if that doesn't help, see Platform support: Access to /dev/uinput."

facts.title: Check before the paste
facts.text: Keys reach whichever login owns the seat, so VOCO asks logind about its originating desktop session before the copy and again just before the keys. An inactive result stops the paste, and so does a locked screen. If logind can't answer, pasting is allowed. The check doesn't lock the session against a later switch.

facts.title: After a key error
facts.text: If the keyboard stops accepting keys, VOCO releases Shift and drops the device, and the next paste creates a fresh one.

facts.title: The companion's keyboard
facts.text: On GNOME Wayland, while the companion is attached and the copy GNOME has loaded asks for work, it presses the keys from inside the Shell, so no new device has to settle first. A Shell still running an older copy keeps VOCO's keyboard until the next login.

facts.title: Keys stay on Wayland
facts.text: Even when xclip sets the clipboard on GNOME, the paste keys still go through the companion, the virtual keyboard or, in the snap, GNOME's portal.

facts.title: The snap's keys and shortcut
facts.text: In the snap on GNOME Wayland, the companion's keyboard types when it asks for work. Otherwise GNOME's RemoteDesktop portal does, through a keyboard-only session that exists only while you dictate, once you choose Allow typing. Its shortcut is the companion's grab, or VOCO's entry in GNOME's keyboard shortcuts, which calls VOCO over D-Bus.
